newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Austria CA sale crisis drags on.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Austria CA sale crisis drags on.

text.p: Austria's coalition government sought to extricate itself from a crisis that could topple it on Monday as the ill-fated privatisation of the country's second bank Creditanstalt looked likely to drag on into 1997.

In separate interviews, Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and his Finance Minister Viktor Klima moved to head off conservative threats of an emergency session of parliament and a no-confidence vote if Klima backed a takeover bid from "socialist" Bank Austria.

"I believe that the coalition will hold together. And that we will reach a sensible decision (on Creditanstalt) in January when Viktor Klima has completed his evaluation of the bids and held additional talks," Vranitzky told magazine News.

Klima, speaking to current affairs weekly Profil, floated the idea of reopening the bidding for conservative stronghold Creditanstalt to give interested parties an opportunity to improve their offers without drawing in fresh partners.
"If possible we will decide this month -- without endangering the coalition. But if there is a reason not to decide before year-end, then we won't do it," Klima said.
Previously, he had insisted he would wind up the sale of the state's 70 percent of ordinary shares by year-end, closing what has become an embarrassing chapter for Austria.

Klima, the third finance minister to tackle the privatisation in the past six years, appeared to be on track to meet his target until market leader Bank Austria entered the fray shortly before the December 16 deadline for bids.

"Red" Bank Austria's offer for the "black" conservative Creditanstalt split the coalition of Social Democrats and rightist People's Party down the middle, raising the spectre of a repeat of last year's snap general election.
According to a weekend opinion poll, both parties are bumping along at popularity lows while the far-right Freedom Party would be the biggest beneficiary of an early election.
"A sensible solution will not hinge on 'red' and 'black' banks but on sound banking economics," Vranitzky said.

Bank Austria has outbid its rivals for control of the nation's most traditional financial institution by more than one billion schillings ($91 million), reportedly putting up some 16 billion. The state's holding is worth 14.5 billion at market prices.
"This is no way to run a privatisation. You can't have a tender and then reopen it because the winner doesn't satisfy political expediency," said an inernational analyst, who declined to be named.

Bank Austria, effectively controlled by the City of Vienna, is up against a group led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali, the conservatives' favoured choice, and 79-year-old entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek, an unfancied dark horse.
The finance ministry was tight-lipped on Monday, leaving the three bidders in the dark about its next move.
"We have had no official word from the finance minister. We are trying to get some sort of explanation," said a spokesman for the EA-Generali consortium.

Austrian daily Der Standard reported the group, which includes savings bank Die Erste Oesterriechische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian), Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana, hoped to raise an extra three billion schillings.
"It looks like the government is giving itself a little more time to persuade the consortium to pay up," said Gerhard Auer, an analyst at ICE Securities in London. ($1=10.95 Schilling)
